sections.heading: 07 — Plain English Glossary
sections.intro:
Every technical term introduced across this knowledge package, defined the way the source material
defines it. Terms are alphabetical.

---

subsections.body:
**AED** — an automated external defibrillator, used interchangeably with "defibrillator" in the
source material: the device that analyzes heart rhythm and advises whether a shock is needed.
subsections.heading: A

subsections.body:
**Cold water shock** — the sudden loss of the ability to control breathing on entering cold water.
Fighting the sensation, rather than floating through it, is what the source material describes as
the actual mechanism of drowning.
subsections.heading: C

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `AmXN6YjxtII`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AmXN6YjxtII
- **Upload date:** 2026-06-23
- **Duration:** 01:08
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/AmXN6YjxtII.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a step-by-step response when a child has collapsed and is not responding, from checking breathing through AED shock delivery
- **Emergencies:** a child who has collapsed and is not responding or breathing normally
- **Procedures:** sending someone for a nearby defibrillator while checking breathing by looking, listening, and feeling for up to 10 seconds, giving five rescue breaths if the child is not breathing, then compressions with one hand to one-third of body depth, in a 15-compressions-to-2-breaths cycle, continued until the AED arrives, AED/defibrillator use on a child, pediatric pads if available, otherwise adult pads, placed one to the left of the chest midline and one directly opposite on the back, then following the device's shock-advised / no-shock-advised prompt and resuming CPR after any shock
- **Important concepts:** one-handed compressions to one-third body depth as the child-specific adaptation of adult CPR technique
subsections.heading: 1. Child Collapses & Not Breathing — What To Do (CPR + AED)

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `dLz7tn-bR9w`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dLz7tn-bR9w
- **Upload date:** 2026-07-19
- **Duration:** 00:47
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/dLz7tn-bR9w.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a 2025 guideline change stating CPR should be started on a bed rather than delaying to move the person to the floor first
- **Emergencies:** someone found collapsed in a bed, not breathing normally
- **Procedures:** check breathing for up to 10 seconds; if not breathing normally, call 999 (the source's emergency number) immediately, per the stated 2025 guidelines, keep the person on the bed rather than moving them to a hard floor first — remove pillows, kneel beside them, start compressions immediately, pushing slightly deeper to compensate for the soft mattress
- **Important concepts:** "starting now beats starting perfectly" as the stated rationale for the guideline change
subsections.heading: 2. CPR in a Bed? Yes – New CPR Guidelines Explained!

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `daEErJU36-4`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=daEErJU36-4
- **Upload date:** 2026-07-14
- **Duration:** 01:00
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/daEErJU36-4.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the distinction between a heart attack (circulation problem) and cardiac arrest (electrical problem), and the different response each calls for
- **Emergencies:** heart attack — a blocked artery stopping blood reaching the heart muscle, person usually conscious, breathing, and talking, cardiac arrest — the heart stops pumping altogether, person is unresponsive and not breathing normally
- **Procedures:** for a heart attack — sit the person down, keep them calm, call emergency medical services, and give any medication they have been told by their doctor to take, for cardiac arrest — call emergency medical services immediately, start CPR immediately, and get a defibrillator if one is nearby
- **Important concepts:** heart attack framed as a circulation (plumbing) problem versus cardiac arrest as an electrical problem, as the core distinguishing model
subsections.heading: 3. Heart Attack vs Cardiac Arrest: The Difference Could Save a Life

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `-q_O1aLYXlw`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-q_O1aLYXlw
- **Upload date:** 2026-07-28
- **Duration:** 01:06
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/-q_O1aLYXlw.txt`
- **Main subjects:** correcting the common instinct to tilt the head back during a nosebleed, and the stated correct technique instead
- **Emergencies:** a nosebleed
- **Procedures:** lean forward, not back, to avoid sending blood down the throat, pinch the soft part of the nose just below the bony bridge, and hold firm, continuous pressure for 10 minutes without releasing to check, staying seated upright and breathing through the mouth, optionally apply a cold compress to the bridge of the nose or back of the neck, if still bleeding after 10 minutes, pinch for another 10 minutes, seek medical help if bleeding hasn't stopped after 30 minutes, if it is heavy, or if the nosebleed followed a head injury
- **Important concepts:** none recorded
subsections.heading: 4. How to Stop a Nosebleed (The Right Way) 🩸 #firstaid

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `MH5zM1q0RlU`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH5zM1q0RlU
- **Upload date:** 2026-08-11
- **Duration:** 00:56
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/MH5zM1q0RlU.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why a bystander should not go into the water after a struggling swimmer, and what to do instead
- **Emergencies:** someone struggling or drowning in open water
- **Procedures:** call the emergency number (999 in the source) and ask for the coast guard if at the coast, or fire rescue if inland (river, lake, or canal), shout at the casualty to float — head back, ears in the water, relax — to buy time, throw anything buoyant (a ring, a body board, an empty bottle, a cool bag), or reach with a towel, branch, or rope while lying flat, staying low, and keeping weight back to avoid being pulled in, if you fall in yourself, float rather than fight the water
- **Important concepts:** "reach, throw, do not go" as the source's stated governing rule for water rescue, cold water shock named as the mechanism that "takes your breathing away," with fighting it described as what actually drowns people
subsections.heading: 5. Reach, Throw, Don't Go — what to do if someone's struggling in water

sections.body:
**Contrary to the common instinct to tilt the head back, the correct technique for a nosebleed is
to lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose (not the bony bridge) with firm, uninterrupted
pressure for 10 minutes.** `[00:00]` "Stop tilting your head back during a nose bleed... you need
to lean forward, not back... pinch the soft part of your nose just below the bony bridge... hold
for firm pressure for 10 minutes straight. And we're not going to let go."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]` Stated reason to avoid tilting back: it "sends blood down your throat, which can make
you feel sick or even vomit." Escalation thresholds given: seek medical help "if the bleeding won't
stop after 30 minutes, or if it's heavy, or if it's followed because you've actually hit your head"
— i.e., a nosebleed following a head injury. `[01:02]` The clip closes mid-sentence on a follow
prompt rather than additional first-aid content.
sections.heading: Why tilting back is wrong, and when to escalate

sections.body:

sections.body:
**When a child collapses and is not responding, the source's protocol is: send someone for a
defibrillator, check breathing for up to 10 seconds, give five rescue breaths if not breathing,
then begin one-handed compressions to one-third body depth in a 15-compressions-to-2-breaths
cycle, continuing until the AED arrives and its prompts can be followed.** `[00:00]` "You look,
listen, and feel for 10 seconds. If they're not breathing, you're going to give five rescue
breaths. Then you're going to start the compressions using one hand pushing down 1/3 of body
depth. You're going to do 15 compressions and then two breaths."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]` Pad choice: pediatric pads if available, adult pads if not. Adult-pad placement is
specified precisely — "the first one is going to the left of the midline of the chest," and "the
second one is going to go straight behind that on their back." `[01:01]` The device analyzes and
announces "shock advised or no shock advised"; if advised, the responder pushes the shock button,
allows the shock, "and then carry on with your CPR."
sections.heading: AED use and pad placement

sections.body:
**Per the source's stated 2025 guideline update, CPR should be started immediately on a bed rather
than delaying to move the person to a hard floor first, compensating for the soft mattress by
pushing slightly deeper.** `[00:00]` "The new guidelines state it's better to start CPR on the bed
than to delay... don't drag them off, take the pillows away, kneel beside them, and start
compressions straight away."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]` The prior practice, as described: "we used to be told that a soft mattress stops you
pushing deep enough, so we had to move them to a hard floor first." The stated reason for the
change: "moving someone wastes precious seconds, and every second without CPR lowers the chance of
survival." The source frames the trade-off directly: **"starting now beats starting perfectly."**

sections.body:
**A heart attack and a cardiac arrest are different emergencies needing different responses: a
heart attack is a circulation problem where the person is usually conscious and talking and needs
to be sat down, kept calm, and given their own medication while emergency services are called; a
cardiac arrest is an electrical problem where the person is unresponsive and not breathing, and
needs immediate CPR and a defibrillator.** `[00:00]` "A heart attack is a circulation problem. It's
a blocked artery that stops blood reaching the heart muscle... Whereas a cardiac arrest is an
electrical problem. The heart stops pumping all together."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
| | Heart attack | Cardiac arrest |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism (as stated) | Circulation problem — blocked artery | Electrical problem — heart stops pumping |
| Consciousness | Usually conscious, breathing, talking | Unresponsive |
| Common signs named | Chest pain or pain spreading to arm/jaw, sweaty/clammy, feeling sick | Not breathing normally |
| Immediate action (as stated) | Sit down, keep calm, call EMS, give own prescribed medication | Call EMS now, start CPR now, get a defibrillator |

`[00:00]` "So conscious and talking, heart attack. Unresponsive and not breathing, cardiac arrest.
Start CPR now."
sections.heading: Distinguishing the two at a glance

sections.body:
Heart attack: chest pain or pain radiating through the arm or jaw, sweating/clamminess, feeling
sick, while conscious and breathing. Cardiac arrest: unresponsive, not breathing normally.
